title: SE enablement - messaging & demo practice
summary: Internal SE/AE practice session to align on messaging, run through a short demo script, and rehearse answers to common competitive and security questions. Focus on highlighting Redwood's production-first positioning, deterministic serving, and routing/fallback story.
next_steps: Maya to share updated demo deck and script (link) by 2026-10-07
Owen to record a 6-min canned demo video for onboarding by 2026-10-14
Luis to update competitive battlecard with Anthropic/OpenAI notes by 2026-10-09
action_items: Maya: Share demo deck + sample prompts (due 2026-10-07)
Owen: Produce short demo recording and upload to internal drive (due 2026-10-14)
Luis: Revise competitive battlecard and add FAQ responses (due 2026-10-09)
Casey: Prepare two customer objection roleplays for next session (due 2026-10-11)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey team, thanks for joining — quick housekeeping, today's 60 minute practice, we'll do messaging -> competitive -> run through a five minute demo script and then rapid fire objections.
[00:15] Owen (SE): Sounds good, I'll jump in on the demo parts and the performance/cost bits.
[00:30] Casey (New AE): Quick question, do we want to keep the opening pitch the same as last quarter or try the new one Luis drafted?
[00:45] Luis (PM): I think keep the new one — shorter, more production-first. "We help engineering teams ship predictable, cost-effective inference so they can focus on product, not ops."
[01:05] Jordan (AE): Works. Maybe add the bit about dedicated vs hosted early so prospects know options.
[01:20] Maya: Good call. Owen if you want to take the dedicated vs hosted talking points?
[01:30] Owen: Sure. Hosted is our fastest time-to-value, metered pricing, great for prototypes and small scale. Dedicated is for customers needing predictable throughput and data isolation — commit capacity, autoscaling, SLA-backed latency. Private is when they need VPC/on-prem and key management.
[01:55] Priya (AE): How do we handle the latency vs cost question? Pros always ask "why would I pay more for dedicated?"
[02:10] Owen: Short answer: predictability and per-token unit economics at scale. For example, with batching, KV cache and quantization profiles we can often reduce per-token cost substantially on Dedicated. But if you need single-digit tail latency you might trade cost for performance. Use the epic example: retail checkout vs back-office summarization.
[02:45] Maya: Okay demo flow — Owen you'll demo the inference flow: API call, routing, fallback, and a quick benchmark note.
[02:55] Owen: Right. I'll start with the simple create request; show how routing can send requests to a cheaper variant unless tail latency is required, then we failover to a higher tier. Also mention prefix caching and KV cash — uh, KV cache (laughs) — sometimes transcripts show K-V cash.
[03:25] Samir (AE): On security questions, we get asked about SOC2 and KMS — what's the crisp answer?
[03:35] Luis: We highlight SOC 2 Type II, SAML/SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and key management options (customer-managed KMS or HSM for Private). If they're particularly sensitive, Private with customer KMS is the path.
[03:50] Casey: Roleplay time — Jordan, you be the skeptical engineering manager, I'll be the AE.
[04:05] Jordan (roleplay): "We run in multiple regions and have strict residency. How do you handle data residency and on-prem?"
[04:20] Casey: "We offer Private deployments with a customer-controlled control plane and can deploy into your VPC. We also support on-prem packages for air-gapped environments. We can bring audit logs and KMS integration to the table; we usually start with a security review and proof-of-concept."
[04:45] Jordan: "What about performance — will it match cloud?"
[04:55] Owen: "Performance is dependent on hardware selection and kernel optimizations. Our runtime chooses kernels and quantization profiles; with the right hardware and config we hit sub-100ms token times on common sequence lengths. We'll run benchmarks during POC and capture tail latency in the console."
[05:15] Priya: Good. A few competitive gotchas we should prep for?
[05:25] Luis: Anthropic — emphasize safety tooling and structured output; OpenAI — call out cost predictability and private deployment options; BentoML/Builder.ai — they may say 'we can self-serve infra' — answer with our unified runtime + managed ops and observability which reduces TCO.
[05:50] Maya: Okay demo practice: Owen run the exact script and I'll interrupt with buyer objections. Try to keep it to five minutes.
[06:05] Owen: Starting... "Here's a quick walkthrough: a request hits the Redwood API, policy-based router evaluates latency/cost/region and routes to the best model variant; if capacity constrained, we automatically fallback to a compatible variant; requests leverage prefix and KV cache to speed up repeated contexts; console shows token-level cost and per-route latency."
[06:30] Casey (interrupting): "What about hallucinations — how do we reassure them?"
[06:40] Owen: "We tie hallucination risk to model choice and prompt engineering, and we provide evals and quality monitoring to detect regressions. We can pin model versions and run rollouts with canary checks; plus tooling to rerank or post-process outputs."
[07:05] Jordan: "And the pricing example? Customers always want numbers."
[07:12] Owen: "We'll say: hosted is metered per-token; typical gen workload X averages Y cents per 1k tokens; Dedicated is committed monthly with lower unit costs at scale — we will provide a benchmark spreadsheet during quoting. Avoid hard numbers unless you confirm their target tpm and sequence length."
[07:40] Maya: Luis, how aggressive should AEs be around quantization and accuracy tradeoffs?
[07:50] Luis: Recommend conservative language: suggest quantization profiles as recommended by our Optimize toolkit and flag potential quality delta — offer to run a sample eval set before moving to quantized model.
[08:05] Priya: There's always the "we already have infra" objection — how do we differentiate?
[08:15] Owen: Focus on ops cost, observability, and predictable SLAs. The cost of running and optimizing inference across hardware, maintaining kernels, and building routing/fallback logic is non-trivial. We offer the runtime + orchestration + console. Also point to case study: RetailCorp saved 32% per-token after batching and caching optimizations during their Dedicated POC (note: placeholder for internal slide).
[08:45] Maya: Good. Quick notes on demo UX: keep the console open, show token-level breakdown, show rollout page quickly, and then a single example of fallback working. Also call out the canary/A-B deploy flow.
[09:05] Owen: Demo now: "Opening console... here you see per-route latency, token cost, and a recent regression alert tied to a prompt set. Click on the deployment and you can trigger a canary rollout with auto-fallback." (sound of mouse clicks, muted)
[09:35] Casey: That felt a bit scripted; maybe weave a customer problem in first — like 'we observed high tail latencies on invoices' — then show how routing fixes it.
[09:50] Jordan: Also rehearse the 'we need data residency' line — make sure mention of Private's KMS and audit logs is quick.
[10:05] Maya: We're 10 minutes in, team — two more demo runs, then rapid-fire QA. Owen, run it once more but shorter.
[10:20] Owen: Short version: "We provide a unified API, routing policies for latency/cost/region, automated prefix/KV cache, and deployment modes (hosted/dedicated/private). For security: SOC2, SAML, RBAC and customer-managed KMS available."
[10:45] Priya (objection practice): "We are concerned about vendor lock-in if we use Redwood."
[10:55] Owen: "We recommend building abstractions in product to make model switching easier; we support model versioning and exportable metrics and evals — the goal is portability plus the operator efficiency of our runtime. Also highlight the open model catalog and ability to run in customer-owned infra for Private deployments."
[11:25] Maya: Great. Quick competitive flashcards — Luis, give us the top 3 points for Anthropic and OpenAI.
[11:35] Luis: Anthropic: safety & helpfulness focus; call out our structured outputs and eval hooks as parity. OpenAI: wide adoption and model quality; call out our deployment flexibility and unit cost controls as differentiators.
[11:55] Casey: Any tricky legal/procurement questions we should prep?
[12:05] Maya: They ask about data retention and logs — say we support customizable retention windows and can exclude logs for Private. Also mention standard enterprise contracts and enterprise support options.
[12:30] Jordan: Roleplay: I'm a CISO who wants to know about auditability.
[12:40] Maya: "We provide detailed audit logs at the request level, integrated with your SIEM. For Private we can integrate with your KMS/HSM and provide full control of keys. We also support SAML SSO and RBAC for least privilege."
[13:05] Owen: Minor demo hiccup — console refresh, fine.
[13:20] Maya: Okay last run — one-minute elevator pitch each, then close. Owen, yours?
[13:30] Owen: "Redwood helps engineering teams ship LLM features with consistent performance across hosted, dedicated and private deployments. Our runtime optimizes for throughput and latency, and our console makes costs and regressions visible, letting you run reliable production inference without building the stack yourself."
[13:55] Maya: Casey?
[14:00] Casey: "We make inference predictable and economical; if you need SLAs or private networking we have Dedicated and Private options to meet the bar."
[14:15] Jordan: Nice. Wrap-up — recap next steps and action items.
[14:25] Maya: Recap: I'll send the updated deck and demo script; Owen will produce a short demo recording; Luis will refresh the competitive battlecard. Schedule follow-up peer review for next week. Any final questions?
[14:40] Priya: None from me.
[14:45] Maya: Thanks everyone, great practice. End.
